ap_calculus_bc-m01.stem: Let $y=f(x)$ be the solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=g(x)-y$ with $f(0)=1$, where the graph of $g$, consisting of line segments, is shown. Euler's method with two steps of equal size $h=2$ starting at $x=0$ is used to approximate $f(4)$. What is the approximation?

stimulus.description: Graph of g, consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Uses the slope at the right endpoint of each step, g(x + h) - y, instead of the left endpoint.
Uses step size 1 for two steps and ends at x = 2 instead of x = 4.
Step 1: y1 = y0 + 2(g(0) - y0). Step 2: y2 = y1 + 2(g(2) - y1), with g read from the graph.
Leaves out the -y term and adds only the values of g.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_bc
blueprint.concept: Apply Euler's method when the slope depends on x through a graph and on y through the equation
student_thinking: Read g(0) and g(2) from the graph
Compute the first Euler step using the slope g(0) - y0
Use the new y value in the second step with the slope g(2) - y1

key_conditions.condition: Euler's method uses the slope at the left endpoint of each step
key_conditions.evidence: definition of Euler's method with step size h

verification.independent_path: two Euler steps recomputed with floating-point arithmetic on the interpolated graph (independent of the exact rationals)

ap_calculus_bc-m02.stem: The third-degree Maclaurin polynomial $P_3$ of a function $f$ with derivatives of all orders is used to estimate $f(1.4)$. The fourth derivative of $f$ is graphed on $0\le x\le 3$ and consists of line segments, as shown. Use the Lagrange error bound to find the least upper bound for the error $|f(1.4)-P_3(1.4)|$ that the graph supports.

stimulus.description: Graph of f^(4)(x), consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Divides by 3! instead of 4!.
Uses the largest signed value of the graph on [0, 1.4] instead of the largest absolute value.
M x^4/4! with M = the maximum of |f^(4)| on [0, a] read from the graph, evaluated with a calculator.
Takes the maximum over the whole graph, not only over [0, 1.4].

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_bc
blueprint.concept: Apply the Lagrange error bound with a bound read from a graph at a non-integer point
student_thinking: Read the largest absolute value of f^(4) on [0, a] from the graph

key_conditions.condition: |f^(4)| <= M on [0, a] for the maximum absolute value read from the graph
key_conditions.evidence: the graph is piecewise linear so the maximum occurs at a vertex or at the endpoint a

misconceptions.description: uses a maximum from outside [0, a]

verification.independent_path: maximum absolute value from a 2000-point grid on [0, a] (independent of vertex reading)

ap_calculus_bc-m03.stem: A curve in the $xy$-plane is given by $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t)$ for $0\le t\le 8$. The graphs of $x$ and $y$ as functions of $t$ are shown and each consists of line segments. What is the value of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at $t=5$?

stimulus.description: Graphs of x(t) and y(t), each consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Subtracts the derivatives, y' - x'.
Multiplies the two derivatives, x' y', instead of dividing.
dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt); the slopes of the two graphs at t = 5 are y' = -5/2 and x' = 3/2.
Divides the positions y(t)/x(t) instead of the rates of change.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_bc
blueprint.concept: Compute dy/dx for parametric equations from the graphs of x(t) and y(t)
student_thinking: Read the slope of the graph of x and of the graph of y at the given t

key_conditions.condition: dx/dt is not zero at the given time, so dy/dx exists
key_conditions.evidence: the slope of the graph of x is nonzero on the segment containing t

verification.independent_path: difference quotient of y over difference quotient of x with step 1e-6 on the interpolated graphs (independent of reading slopes)

ap_calculus_bc-m04.stem: A particle moves in the $xy$-plane. The graphs of $x'(t)$ and $y'(t)$ for $0\le t\le 8$ are shown and each consists of line segments. What is the speed of the particle at $t=4$?

stimulus.description: Graphs of x'(t) and y'(t), each consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Adds the absolute values of the components instead of using the Pythagorean combination.
Does not take the square root: (x')^2 + (y')^2.
Reports x'(t) alone.
Speed = sqrt((x')^2 + (y')^2) with x'(4) and y'(4) read from the graphs.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_bc
blueprint.concept: Find speed from the graphs of the two velocity components
student_thinking: Read x'(a) from the first graph and y'(a) from the second

key_conditions.condition: speed equals the magnitude of the velocity vector
key_conditions.evidence: definition of speed for planar motion

verification.independent_path: math.hypot of the numerically interpolated components at t = a (independent of the Pythagorean triple used to build the graphs)

ap_calculus_bc-m05.stem: The function $f$ has derivatives of all orders and $f(0)=1$. The graph of $f'$, consisting of line segments, is shown for $0\le x\le 4$. Let $P_2$ be the second-degree Maclaurin polynomial for $f$. What is $P_2(3)$?

stimulus.description: Graph of f', consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Uses f''(0) x/2 instead of f''(0) x^2/2.
Leaves out the factorial: f''(0) x^2 instead of f''(0) x^2/2!.
P2(x) = f(0) + f'(0) x + f''(0) x^2/2!; f'(0) is the height of the graph at 0 and f''(0) is the slope of the first segment.
Uses f'(3) from the graph instead of f'(0) for the linear term.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_bc
blueprint.concept: Build a Maclaurin polynomial using f'(0) and f''(0) read from the graph of f'
student_thinking: Read f'(0) from the graph and f''(0) as the slope of the graph of f' at 0

key_conditions.condition: f''(0) is the slope of f' on the first segment because f' is linear near 0
key_conditions.evidence: the graph consists of line segments

misconceptions.description: reads f' at the wrong point
uses x instead of x squared

verification.independent_path: polynomial evaluated numerically from numerically interpolated heights and finite-difference slope of f' (independent of the exact vertices)

ap_calculus_bc-m06.stem: A particle moves in the $xy$-plane. Its position at $t=0$ is $(5,5)$. The graphs of the velocity components $x'(t)$ and $y'(t)$ are shown for $0\le t\le 8$, each consisting of line segments. What is the position of the particle at $t=4$?

stimulus.description: Graphs of x'(t) and y'(t), each consisting of line segments connecting the plotted vertices.

options.why: Reports the displacement only and forgets the initial position.
Swaps the coordinates: the x-coordinate and the y-coordinate are reversed.
Position = initial position + the integral of velocity: x(b) = x(0) + area under x', y(b) = y(0) + area under y'.
Adds the velocity components at t = 4 to the initial position instead of integrating.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_bc
blueprint.concept: Find a position vector from initial position and the graphs of both velocity components
student_thinking: Recognize that each coordinate equals its initial value plus the signed area under its velocity graph
Compute the signed area under each graph from 0 to the given time
Combine the coordinates as an ordered pair

key_conditions.condition: position equals initial position plus the integral of velocity for each component
key_conditions.evidence: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus applied to each coordinate

verification.independent_path: numerical quadrature of each interpolated velocity component plus the initial position (independent of trapezoid areas)
